items.informal_statement: For any real Banach space $E$, mean $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$, positive variance $v > 0$, and measurable function $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$, the Bochner integral of $f$ with respect to the Gaussian measure $\gamma_{\mu,v}$ satisfies $\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x) \, d\gamma_{\mu,v}(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v}} e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2v}} f(x) \, dx$, where the right-hand side uses the Lebesgue integral of the product of the Gaussian density and $f$.

items.informal_statement: For any real number $\mu$ and positive real number $v > 0$, the Lebesgue integral of the Gaussian probability density function $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2v}\right)$ over $\mathbb{R}$ equals 1, i.e., $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2v}\right) dx = 1$.

items.informal_statement: The integral of a continuous linear map $ L : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ with respect to the Gaussian measure on $ \mathbb{R} $ with mean $ \mu $ and variance $ v $ is equal to $ L(\mu) $, i.e., $ \int_{\mathbb{R}} L(x) \, d\text{Gaussian}(\mu, v)(x) = L(\mu) $.

items.informal_statement: For any linear map $ L : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $, the integral of $ L(x) $ with respect to the Gaussian measure on $ \mathbb{R} $ with mean $ \mu $ and variance $ v \geq 0 $ is equal to $ L(\mu) $. The Gaussian measure is defined as the Dirac measure $ \delta_\mu $ when $ v = 0 $, and as the Lebesgue measure with density $ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2v}\right) $ when $ v > 0 $.
